stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Reach Tentative 60-Day Ceasefire Extension, Hormuz Reopening Terms Set
stories.summary:
U.S. and Iranian negotiators reached a tentative agreement Thursday to extend the 3-month-old ceasefire by 60 days and launch a new round of talks on Iran's nuclear program, according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter. Vice President JD Vance confirmed the tentative deal but said it remained unclear whether President Trump would approve it, noting that negotiators were still working through disputed language points.

Under the emerging memorandum of understanding, Iran would be prohibited from imposing tolls on the Strait of Hormuz and required to remove all mines from the critical waterway within 30 days. In return, the U.S. would gradually lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and relax sanctions, allowing Iran to sell more oil. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted oil prices could 'come down very quickly' once a final deal is in place.

Iran had not publicly confirmed the deal as of Friday. The ceasefire has been under strain, with Kuwait intercepting Iranian missiles less than 24 hours before the agreement was announced. Iran has been allowing roughly two dozen commercial vessels daily through the Strait — compared with more than 100 before the war — and had established a formal gatekeeper agency to charge tolls, prompting a fresh round of U.S. sanctions this week.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil and natural gas flows, has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, driving energy prices sharply higher globally. A finalized deal would represent a significant diplomatic development, though both sides have previously traded accusations of bad faith, and the agreement still requires approval from both Trump and Iran's leadership.

stories.headline: Louisiana Passes New Congressional Map Eliminating Majority-Black District Following Supreme Court Ruling
stories.summary:
Louisiana lawmakers approved a new congressional map Friday that eliminates one of the state's two majority-Black U.S. House districts while positioning Republicans to potentially pick up a seat. The state Senate passed the measure 28-10, and Republican Gov. Jeff Landry is expected to sign it into law.

The move follows an April 30 Supreme Court ruling that struck down Louisiana's existing court-ordered map — drawn in 2024 to comply with the Voting Rights Act — as an illegal racial gerrymander. That ruling weakened the landmark 1965 Voting Rights Act and intensified a national redistricting battle, with Louisiana among several Southern states now redrawing maps to benefit Republicans ahead of midterm elections. President Trump has made protecting the GOP's slim House majority a priority.

Republican bill sponsor state Sen. Jay Morris insisted the new map was drawn along partisan, not racial, lines, saying he directed demographers to exclude racial data and told lawmakers he was intentionally concentrating Democrats — not Black voters specifically — into a single district. Democratic state Sen. Sam Jenkins countered that the map amounts to racial gerrymandering that will face further legal challenges: 'I think it's a racially gerrymandered district that's going to get us into a lot of trouble here,' he said. Morris replied, 'Agree to disagree.'

Republicans currently hold four of Louisiana's six congressional seats. The approved 5-1 map was chosen over a more aggressive 6-0 option, which Republicans deemed riskier because it would have required adding more Black voters to GOP-held districts. Legal challenges to the new map are considered likely.

stories.headline: Russia Warns of Escalating Strikes on Kyiv as Putin Seeks to Revive Domestic War Narrative
stories.summary:
Russia has warned of 'consistent and systematic' missile strikes on Kyiv and called for foreign embassies to evacuate the Ukrainian capital, signaling President Vladimir Putin's intention to sharply escalate aerial attacks. Analysts say Putin is seeking to reverse sagging domestic approval ratings and counter growing Russian war fatigue as the conflict enters its fifth year with battlefield advances stalled.

Russia's front-line gains, which had accelerated in 2025, have largely ground to a halt in recent months. The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War assessed that 'the character of the war is shifting in favor of Ukrainian forces, at least for now,' noting that Ukrainian forces have reclaimed some ground and are employing new tactics to break out of positional warfare. Three people were injured Friday in a Russian strike on the city of Zaporizhzhia, with residential buildings damaged.

Moscow has paired its escalatory rhetoric with large-scale nuclear force drills and warnings to European allies against what the Kremlin characterizes as their involvement in Ukrainian drone attacks. Putin's stated objective of quickly capturing the eastern Donetsk region remains unfulfilled, and the battlefield stalemate is undermining his domestic political messaging.

The warnings come amid the broader context of the ongoing U.S.-Iran war, which has diverted Western and U.S. attention and resources. European allies have been ramping up support to Ukraine in that environment, and the prospect of intensified strikes on Kyiv raises the stakes for civilian casualties and international response.

stories.headline: Hegseth Reassures Asian Allies on U.S. Commitment at Shangri-La Dialogue, Calls for Higher Defense Spending
stories.summary:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth addressed the Shangri-La Dialogue security summit in Singapore on Saturday, seeking to reassure Asia-Pacific allies that the United States was not abandoning the region despite its military commitments in the Iran war. Hegseth rejected suggestions that global obligations meant 'turning our backs' on Asia, saying the U.S. can 'do two things at one time' and was working 'quietly but very strongly' with regional partners.

Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi pressed Hegseth directly, warning that some countries might 'underestimate' U.S. commitment and seek to 'drive a wedge' between Washington and its allies. Hegseth also faced questions about the U.S. suspension of a $14 billion arms package to Taiwan — done to conserve munitions for the Iran conflict — and insisted the U.S. remained in a 'very strong position' on its overall munitions stockpile. He said he would 'very much decouple' the Taiwan arms issue from broader alliance commitments.

Hegseth used the forum to reiterate demands that Asian allies spend at least 3.5 percent of GDP on defense, praising Japan, South Korea, Australia, and the Philippines for recent increases in military spending and cooperation. His address came hours after Vietnam's President To Lam, delivering the summit's keynote, called for adherence to international law and more dialogue to manage U.S.-China competition, warning that flashpoints like the Strait of Hormuz show how regional crises can rapidly disrupt global trade and energy.

The summit comes weeks after President Trump's positive meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing, adding complexity to U.S. messaging on deterrence versus engagement. Hegseth's emphasis on 'hard power' over 'rules-based order' rhetoric drew implicit contrast with the multilateral tone favored by several other summit participants.
